title: The Waiting Game
reviewNotes: All forty diagrams and native 109-second ...h2 root reviewed. Rh8 checks all six legal bishop defenses, each answered by Rxh2 mate in supported seven-piece positions. Native first-rank return is Rb1, not Ra1; its immediate eight-piece stalemate is independently saved by legal move generation. Earlier larger queen sacrifice and king walk remain outside proof.
transcript: This looks like a free queen, but you cannot take it because otherwise black is going to capture back and actually the bishop and the two extra pawns are going to be enough to hold back the rook and pawn. But white comes up with an incredible idea. Rook to B1. Realizing that if the queen ever moves, this would be a checkmate in one move. And if black tries to move away with a check, after the white king takes, black still has legal moves, so this is not a stalemate and white would win, which means that this position >> [music] >> becomes a waiting game. Black is going to try to run out of available moves so that he can then sacrifice the queen and stalemate. So black plays pawn to C4. And of course we don't want to take this pawn or the black queen is going to escape with a check. Instead, white plays the seemingly mysterious king to C6, walking away from the action, but foreseeing a beautiful idea. Black continues [music] to push the pawns, trying to run out of moves, and white continues with king to B7. And finally black plays pawn to H3, running out of all available moves with this pawn. And white finishes this king walk with king to A8. Again, if the queen moves, this would be a checkmate. And if the queen gives a check, black would still have legal moves and not have a stalemate, which is why black has to push the pawn to C3. And now we see the point of playing the king all [music] the way to A8, because after B takes C3, black has no other choice but to finally move the queen. And we have conveniently placed the king in such a way that the only way that black can give a check is on B8. But now, we have opened up the rook to capture back with the [music] rook. But wait a second, black can play pawn to H2. And now if we try to come back with [music] the rook, actually, this is a stalemate. The bishop is pinned and none of these pawns can move. So, this would be a draw. So, has white messed up? Was this plan not good after all? Not exactly. White can play rook to H8, now pinning the pawn to the king. Which means that the only move available to black is to move the bishop. But after black does that, finally, rook to H2 will be a checkmate.
